followUps.question: When would you use a struct over a class?
followUps.answer: Use a struct when the type is small (< 16 bytes), immutable, short-lived, and represents a single value like coordinates or money.
followUps.interviewPitch: I use structs for small, immutable types (under 16 bytes) that represent a single value, like a coordinate or currency. Structs are value types allocated on the stack, which avoids Garbage Collection overhead. However, if the data is large or needs to be mutated, I always use a class to avoid the performance penalty of constantly copying large amounts of data.
followUps.explanation:
**📦 The Sticky Note Analogy:**
• **Struct (A Sticky Note):** If someone asks for your phone number, you don't give them your actual phone. You write it on a tiny sticky note and hand it to them. It's so small and cheap that you don't care about copying it.
• **Class (A Library Book):** If someone wants to read a massive encyclopedia, you don't photocopy all 1,000 pages for them. You just give them the address (the reference pointer) of the library.

**When to use Structs:**
• Very small data (< 16 bytes).
• Immutable data (read-only).
• High-performance loops where you want to avoid triggering the Garbage Collector.
followUps.whyAsked: Tests if you know the practical guidelines, not just the textbook definition.
mistakes: Making structs with mutable fields — leads to confusing bugs when copies are modified.
Using structs for large objects — copy overhead negates stack allocation benefits.
followUps.diagram:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Struct
    S1[Small Value] -.->|Fast Copy| S2[Small Value Copy]
    end
    
    subgraph Class
    C1[Pointer A] --> Obj[(Massive 1GB Object in Heap)]
    C2[Pointer B] --> Obj
    end

followUps.question: What happens when you pass a struct to a method?
followUps.answer: A copy of the struct is made. The method works with the copy, so changes inside the method do NOT affect the original.
followUps.interviewPitch: Because structs are value types, passing them to a method creates a complete bit-by-bit copy. The method receives its own independent version of the struct. Any modifications made inside the method will not affect the original variable. If you explicitly want the method to modify the original struct, you must pass it using the `ref` keyword to pass a pointer instead of a copy.
followUps.explanation:
**🖨️ The Photocopy Analogy:**
Imagine you have a physical paper document.

• **By Value (Default):** You walk over to the photocopier, make an exact copy of the paper, and hand the copy to your coworker. If your coworker spills coffee all over their copy, your original paper is completely safe.
• **By Ref (`ref` keyword):** You hand your coworker the original, one-and-only piece of paper. If they spill coffee on it, it is ruined forever.
followUps.whyAsked: Tests understanding of value type copy semantics — a frequent source of subtle bugs.
mistakes: Expecting struct modifications inside a method to affect the caller — they don't without ref.
Not knowing that boxing a struct (casting to object/interface) creates a heap copy.

followUps.question: Can structs implement interfaces?
followUps.answer: Yes, structs can implement interfaces. But be careful — casting a struct to an interface type causes boxing, which allocates it on the heap.
followUps.interviewPitch: Yes, structs can implement interfaces. However, you have to be extremely careful because casting a struct to an interface causes 'Boxing'. An interface is a reference type, so when you cast a stack-allocated struct to an interface, the runtime allocates memory on the heap and copies the struct into it. This completely defeats the performance benefits of using a struct in the first place.
followUps.explanation:
**📦 The Cardboard Box Analogy:**
Imagine a struct is a loose apple on your desk (The Stack).

An interface is like a shipping label. You can't stick a shipping label directly onto a loose apple. You first have to put the apple into a cardboard box (The Heap), and then put the label on the box.

Putting the apple into the box is called **Boxing**. It takes time, uses cardboard, and creates trash that the Garbage Collector has to clean up later.
followUps.whyAsked: Tests advanced understanding of value types, boxing, and performance implications.
mistakes: Not knowing that interface casting causes boxing — negates the stack benefit.
Forgetting that generic constraints avoid boxing — this is the recommended pattern.
followUps.diagram:
flowchart TD
    A[Struct on Stack] -->|Cast to Interface| B((Boxed on Heap))
    B -->|Garbage Collector| C[Triggers GC overhead!]
    style B fill:#ffcccc,stroke:#cc0000

followUps.question: When would you choose an abstract class over an interface?
followUps.answer: Choose an abstract class when related classes need shared state (fields) or common implementation that they all inherit.
followUps.interviewPitch: I choose an abstract class when classes share a core identity and I want to provide default, shared implementation for some of the methods to avoid code duplication. I use an interface when I want to define a capability or behavior (like `ILoggable` or `IDisposable`) that can be implemented by completely unrelated classes. A class can implement multiple interfaces, but can only inherit from one abstract class.
followUps.explanation:
**🧬 The DNA vs Job Title Analogy:**
• **Abstract Class (DNA):** It defines *what an object IS*. A Dog and a Cat both inherit from the abstract class `Mammal`. They share actual DNA (shared code), like the `Breathe()` method, so you don't have to write `Breathe()` twice.
• **Interface (A Job Title):** It defines *what an object CAN DO*. A `Robot` and a `Human` are completely unrelated species, but they can both implement `IJanitor` and have a `CleanFloor()` method.
followUps.whyAsked: Tests design decision-making — not just knowing the difference, but knowing when to apply each.
mistakes: Defaulting to abstract classes for everything — leads to rigid hierarchies.
Forgetting C# 8 default interface methods — interfaces can now have implementations too.
followUps.diagram:
flowchart TD
    subgraph Abstract Class (Identity)
    A[Abstract: Vehicle] --> B[Car]
    A --> C[Truck]
    end
    
    subgraph Interface (Capability)
    I[Interface: IFlyable] -.-> D[Bird]
    I -.-> E[Airplane]
    I -.-> F[Superman]
    end

followUps.question: Can an interface inherit from another interface?
followUps.answer: Yes, an interface can inherit from one or more other interfaces. The implementing class must implement all members from the entire inheritance chain.
followUps.interviewPitch: Yes, an interface can inherit from one or more other interfaces. This is very useful for composing smaller, specialized interfaces into a larger one without violating the Interface Segregation Principle. When a class implements the derived interface, it is required to implement all the methods from both the child interface and its parent interfaces.
followUps.explanation:
**📄 The Certifications Analogy:**
Imagine getting professional certifications.

• To get your **Master Plumber** certification (`IMasterPlumber`), you are required to first hold the **Basic Plumber** certification (`IPlumber`).
• Therefore, `IMasterPlumber` inherits from `IPlumber`. 
• If a worker claims to be an `IMasterPlumber`, they must prove they know how to do the Master tasks AND the Basic tasks.
followUps.whyAsked: Tests understanding of interface composition and .NET's type hierarchy.
mistakes: Confusing interface inheritance with class inheritance — interfaces support multiple inheritance, classes don't.
Forgetting that the implementing class must implement ALL inherited members.
followUps.diagram:
flowchart BT I2[IReadWriteRepository] -- Inherits --> I1[IReadOnlyRepository] C[UserRepository] -- Implements --> I2 Note over C: Must implement methods
from BOTH interfaces!

followUps.question: What is the IDisposable interface and the `using` statement?
followUps.answer: IDisposable provides a Dispose() method for deterministic cleanup of unmanaged resources. The 'using' statement ensures Dispose() is called automatically, even if an exception occurs.
followUps.interviewPitch: The `IDisposable` interface contains a single method: `Dispose()`. We implement it to explicitly release unmanaged resources like open file handles, database connections, or network sockets, because the Garbage Collector doesn't know how to close them. The `using` statement is a syntactic sugar that ensures `Dispose()` is automatically called the moment the object goes out of scope, even if an exception crashes the code inside the block.
followUps.explanation:
**🚰 The Running Faucet Analogy:**
Imagine turning on the faucet to wash your hands.

• **Without `using`:** You turn on the water. While washing, you slip and fall, hitting your head (An Exception). You are unconscious on the floor, and the water runs forever, eventually flooding your house (A Memory Leak).
• **With `using`:** The faucet has a motion sensor. The absolute millisecond you walk away (or fall down), the sensor automatically shuts off the water. It is a 100% guarantee that the resource is cleaned up.
followUps.whyAsked: Tests if you understand resource management beyond just letting GC handle everything.
mistakes: Thinking Dispose() and GC are the same — Dispose is deterministic, GC is not.
Forgetting to use 'using' — leaked connections are a top cause of production outages.
followUps.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant App
    participant DB as SQL Connection
    
    App->>DB: Open Connection (using)
    App->>App: 💥 Exception occurs!
    Note over App: Code crashes, but...
    App->>DB: Dispose() is AUTOMATICALLY called
    Note over DB: Connection safely closed.

followUps.question: How does GC handle Large Object Heap (LOH) differently?
followUps.answer: Objects >= 85KB are allocated on the LOH. The LOH is only collected during Gen 2 collections and is NOT compacted by default, which can cause fragmentation.
followUps.interviewPitch: The Garbage Collector handles objects larger than 85,000 bytes entirely differently. Instead of placing them in Gen 0, it places them directly into the Large Object Heap (LOH). The LOH is essentially treated as Gen 2 memory because copying huge 10MB arrays around during memory compaction would destroy CPU performance. Because LOH objects are rarely collected and never compacted (by default), rapidly allocating and abandoning large objects causes extreme memory fragmentation and `OutOfMemory` exceptions.
followUps.explanation:
**🚚 The Traffic Jam Analogy:**
• **Gen 0 (Motorcycles):** Small objects are like motorcycles. They are easy to park, easy to move around, and if they get abandoned, a tow truck can snatch them up in 5 seconds.
• **The LOH (18-Wheeler Semi Trucks):** Huge arrays are like massive cargo trucks. If you park an 18-wheeler, it is incredibly difficult and slow to move it again. 

So, the city (The GC) creates a special parking lot just for 18-wheelers (The LOH). Once a truck parks there, the city refuses to ever move it (No Compaction). If you keep driving trucks in and leaving empty spaces between them (Fragmentation), eventually no new trucks will fit, and the city shuts down.
followUps.whyAsked: Tests advanced GC knowledge — important for high-performance .NET services.
mistakes: Not knowing the 85KB threshold — a common interview trick question.
Ignoring ArrayPool for large buffer reuse — simple fix for LOH pressure.
followUps.diagram:
flowchart TD
    Obj[New Object]
    Obj -->|Size < 85kb| S1[Generation 0 (Small Object Heap)]
    Obj -->|Size > 85kb| LOH[Large Object Heap (LOH)]
    
    S1 -.->|Compacted often| GC1[Clean Memory]
    LOH -.->|Never compacted!| GC2[Fragmented Memory Holes]
    style LOH fill:#ffcccc,stroke:#cc0000

followUps.question: What is deferred execution in LINQ?
followUps.answer: Deferred execution means the LINQ query is NOT executed when defined — it runs only when you iterate over the results (foreach, ToList, First, etc.).
followUps.interviewPitch: Deferred execution means that a LINQ query is not actually executed at the exact moment it is written in code. Instead, the query is just a 'recipe'. The actual iteration and evaluation only happens when the query is enumerated (e.g., calling `.ToList()`, putting it in a `foreach` loop, or calling `.Count()`). This is highly efficient because it allows you to build complex queries dynamically before making a single, optimized round-trip to the database.
followUps.explanation:
**🧾 The Restaurant Order Analogy:**
Imagine writing a LINQ query is like telling a waiter what you want to eat.

• **Deferred Execution:** You say, "I want a burger." The waiter writes it on his notepad. He doesn't go to the kitchen yet. You then say, "Actually, add cheese." He updates the notepad. The food is NOT being cooked yet. The food only starts cooking when you finally say, "That's all, submit my order." (`.ToList()` or `.Count()`).
• **Immediate Execution:** If LINQ wasn't deferred, the millisecond you said "I want a burger", the waiter would run to the kitchen and cook it. When you added cheese, he would have to cook an entirely new burger.
followUps.whyAsked: Tests if you understand when queries actually execute — critical for avoiding performance issues.
mistakes: Thinking the query runs when you write .Where() — it doesn't until you enumerate.
Iterating a deferred query multiple times — causes multiple DB round trips.

followUps.question: Can you give an example of when using IEnumerable over a database call causes issues?
followUps.answer: If a repository returns IEnumerable instead of IQueryable, all rows are loaded into memory first, then filtered in C# — potentially loading millions of unnecessary rows.
followUps.interviewPitch: Using `IEnumerable` over a database call (like Entity Framework) causes the N+1 Query Problem or memory exhaustion. When you use `IEnumerable`, the data is pulled into RAM, and any subsequent LINQ filters (like `.Where()`) are executed in C# memory, not in the database. If you use `IQueryable`, the filters are translated into raw SQL, so the database engine does the filtering, and only the exact required rows are sent over the network.
followUps.explanation:
**📚 The Library Analogy:**
Imagine you want to find all books written by Stephen King.

• **`IEnumerable` (The Bad Way):** You rent a massive U-Haul truck. You go to the library, put all 100,000 books from the library into the truck, and drive them to your house (RAM). You then search through them one-by-one in your living room to find the 5 Stephen King books.
• **`IQueryable` (The Good Way):** You call the librarian and say, "Give me only the books by Stephen King." The librarian (The Database Engine) searches their own shelves, and hands you exactly 5 books.
followUps.whyAsked: A real-world performance trap — tests if you've dealt with ORM performance issues.
mistakes: Returning IEnumerable from repositories by default — always prefer IQueryable for DB sources.
Not profiling SQL queries — you won't notice until the table grows large.
followUps.diagram:
flowchart LR
    subgraph IEnumerable (Bad)
    DB1[(SQL DB)] -->|Select * (100,000 rows)| App1[C# RAM]
    App1 -->|Where(x => x.Active)| Result1[5 rows]
    end
    
    subgraph IQueryable (Good)
    DB2[(SQL DB)] -->|Select * Where Active| App2[C# RAM]
    App2 --> Result2[5 rows]
    end
    style App1 fill:#ffcccc,stroke:#cc0000
    style App2 fill:#ccffcc,stroke:#00cc00

followUps.question: What is `ConfigureAwait(false)` and why use it?
followUps.answer: ConfigureAwait(false) tells the awaiter to NOT capture the current SynchronizationContext, allowing the continuation to run on any ThreadPool thread.
followUps.interviewPitch: `ConfigureAwait(false)` tells the awaiter not to capture the current SynchronizationContext. In UI applications (like WPF or WinForms) or older ASP.NET (pre-Core), awaiting a task captures the UI thread so the continuation can resume on that exact same thread. If you don't need to update the UI after the task finishes, using `ConfigureAwait(false)` allows the continuation to resume on any available background thread, improving performance and preventing insidious deadlocks.
followUps.explanation:
**🎭 The VIP Booth Analogy:**
Imagine a popular nightclub (The UI Application).

• **Without `ConfigureAwait(false)`:** A VIP guest (A Thread) leaves their private booth to go to the bathroom (Awaiting a database call). They leave their jacket on the seat to "capture" it. When they get back, they refuse to sit anywhere else but that exact booth. If someone else is sitting there, they freeze and wait forever (A Deadlock).
• **With `ConfigureAwait(false)`:** The guest goes to the bathroom, but tells the bouncer, "I don't care where I sit when I get back." When they return, they just grab the first available stool at the bar (A Background Thread). It's much faster and completely avoids deadlocks.
followUps.whyAsked: Tests deep async understanding — separates juniors from seniors.
mistakes: Using ConfigureAwait(false) in UI event handlers — will crash when updating controls.
Thinking it's required in ASP.NET Core — there's no SynchronizationContext to capture.
followUps.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant UI as UI Thread
    participant B as Background Thread
    
    Note over UI, B: Without ConfigureAwait(false)
    UI->>B: Starts HTTP Request (await)
    Note over UI: UI Thread is blocked/busy
    B-->>UI: Done! Tries to return to UI Thread
    Note over UI, B: 💥 DEADLOCK! UI is busy, Task is waiting for UI.
    
    Note over UI, B: With ConfigureAwait(false)
    UI->>B: Starts HTTP Request (await)
    B-->>B: Done! Resumes on ANY background thread.
    Note over B: ✅ No Deadlock!

followUps.question: Can you use `await` inside a `lock` block?
followUps.answer: No. The compiler prevents it because lock uses thread-affine Monitor which can deadlock with async. Use SemaphoreSlim instead.
followUps.interviewPitch: No, C# completely forbids using the `await` keyword inside a `lock` statement, and the compiler will throw an error. This is because a `lock` is tied to a specific thread. When you `await` a task, the method yields control and the thread is freed to do other work. When the task finishes, it might resume on a completely different thread. If a different thread tries to release a lock that the original thread acquired, the application's synchronization is destroyed. Instead, you must use `SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync()`.
followUps.explanation:
**🔑 The Bathroom Key Analogy:**
• A `lock` block is like taking the physical key to a gas station bathroom. Only YOU (Thread A) can unlock the door when you are done.
• If you are allowed to `await` inside the bathroom, it means you teleport out of the bathroom to do other work, leaving the door locked.
• When the work is done, your clone (Thread B) teleports back to finish the job. But Thread B doesn't have the key! They can't unlock the door! The bathroom is locked forever.

To fix this, we use `SemaphoreSlim`, which is like a bouncer counting people, rather than a physical key tied to a specific person.
followUps.whyAsked: Tests practical async knowledge — a real gotcha developers hit in production.
mistakes: Trying to work around the compiler error — the restriction exists for good reason.
Using lock for async code — always use SemaphoreSlim for async mutual exclusion.
followUps.diagram:
flowchart TD
    T1[Thread 1 acquires lock]
    T1 --> A[Awaits Task (Yields thread)]
    A -.->|Task finishes| T2[Thread 2 resumes execution]
    T2 --> C{Try to release lock}
    C -->|ERROR!| D[Thread 2 didn't acquire it!]
    style D fill:#ffcccc,stroke:#cc0000

followUps.question: What is the `in` parameter modifier?
followUps.answer: The 'in' keyword (C# 7.2) passes a value type by reference but makes it read-only — the method cannot modify it. Used to avoid copying large structs.
followUps.interviewPitch: The `in` parameter modifier is a performance optimization used primarily for large structs. It passes the argument by reference (to avoid the expensive memory allocation of copying a large struct), but enforces strict read-only semantics so the method cannot modify the original value. It acts like the `ref` keyword, but guarantees immutability.
followUps.explanation:
**🖼️ The Museum Painting Analogy:**
Imagine a massive, heavy, priceless painting (A Large Struct).

• **Pass by Value (Default):** A friend asks to see the painting. You hire a forgery artist to paint an exact replica (Allocating Memory), and you ship the replica to your friend.
• **Pass by `ref`:** You ship the actual painting to your friend. But your friend is allowed to draw a mustache on it (Mutate it).
• **Pass by `in`:** Your friend walks into your museum and looks at the original painting behind bulletproof glass. They don't have to copy it, but they are strictly forbidden from touching it (Read-Only).
followUps.whyAsked: Tests knowledge of C# 7.2+ features and performance-conscious coding.
mistakes: Using 'in' for small types like int — the indirection overhead makes it slower.
Confusing 'in' with 'ref readonly' — they are related but 'in' is for parameters.
followUps.diagram:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Pass by Value
    O1[Huge Struct] -->|Copies 1000 bytes| M1[Method]
    end
    
    subgraph Pass by 'in'
    O2[Huge Struct] -.->|Read-Only Pointer| M2[Method]
    end
    style O1 fill:#ffcccc,stroke:#cc0000
    style O2 fill:#ccffcc,stroke:#00cc00

followUps.question: How do reference types behave when passed by value without `ref`?
followUps.answer: The reference (pointer) is copied, but both copies point to the same object on the heap. You can mutate properties, but you cannot reassign the reference to a different object.
followUps.interviewPitch: When you pass a reference type (a class) to a method without the `ref` keyword, you are passing a *copy of the reference*, not a copy of the object itself. Because the copied reference still points to the exact same object on the heap, modifying properties of the object inside the method *will* affect the original. However, if you reassign the variable to a completely `new` object inside the method, it only changes the local copy of the pointer. The caller's pointer will still look at the old object.
followUps.explanation:
**🏠 The House Address Analogy:**
Imagine an object is a physical House (The Heap). The variable is just a piece of paper with the address written on it (The Reference).

When you pass the variable to a method, you write the address on a second piece of paper and hand it to the method.

• **Modifying the object:** The method drives to the address and paints the house blue. When you drive to your address, the house is blue. You share the same house!
• **Reassigning the variable:** The method crosses out the address on their piece of paper and writes down a completely new address (`new User()`). This does NOT magically change what is written on *your* piece of paper. You still point to the old house.
followUps.whyAsked: Tests precise understanding of reference vs value semantics — a common source of confusion.
mistakes: Thinking without ref you can't modify the object — you CAN modify properties, just not reassign.
Thinking ref is needed to pass objects — it's only needed to reassign the reference itself.
followUps.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant M as Method
    participant H as Heap Memory
    
    C->>H: Creates User "Alice"
    C->>M: Passes Address (0x123)
    M->>H: Changes Name to "Bob"
    Note over C, H: Caller sees "Bob"!
    M->>M: Reassigns to NEW User "Charlie" (0x999)
    M-->>C: Returns
    Note over C: Caller STILL sees "Bob" at 0x123!
